title: Our Solar System May Be Trapping Invisible Dark Matter, and Scientists Think They Can Detect It
excerpt: How our solar system traps dark matter may hold the key to better understanding the elusive, hypothetical substance believed to make up the majority of all matter in the universe.
content:
How our solar system traps dark matter may hold the key to better understanding the elusive, hypothetical substance believed to make up the majority of all matter in the universe.

In a recent paper published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics, scientists proposed that dark matter accumulating within celestial bodies could provide a way to test some of the leading explanations for the mysterious material.

The team argues that while slower-moving dark matter particles may be difficult to detect using existing instruments, they could accumulate inside planets and stars at densities sufficient to produce measurable signals. Dark matter does not emit, reflect, or absorb light, rendering it effectively invisible, although its gravitational influence can be observed.

Detecting Dark Matter

As the nature of dark matter remains a mystery, researchers continue to explore how indirect observations might help test competing hypotheses. By considering the properties that dark matter particles might possess, scientists can predict how those particles would interact with ordinary matter and search for evidence of those interactions.

Slower-moving dark matter particles would produce incredibly weak effects individually. However, celestial bodies within our solar system could potentially capture them if they lose even a small amount of energy through interactions with ordinary matter. As these particles accumulate in denser concentrations near the centers of planets and stars, they may collide and annihilate one another.

Such annihilation events could produce other particles, potentially heating the celestial bodies in which the dark matter has accumulated or generating detectable particles that escape into space. The researchers calculated the expected effects of these interactions under two dark matter hypotheses and compared their predictions with observational data.

Seeking Dark Matter Clues

“In this work, we considered four celestial bodies: Earth, the Sun, Jupiter and white dwarfs,” said co-author Gaurav Tomar, of the Center for Quantum Spacetime at Sogang University in South Korea. “There are dedicated experiments, for example, IceCube at the South Pole, looking for neutrinos from the Sun and Earth. For Jupiter and white dwarfs, we considered the heating possibilities.”

Beneath the Antarctic ice, the IceCube Neutrino Observatory searches for evidence of elusive particles known as neutrinos. With extremely small masses and no electric charge, neutrinos interact only rarely with ordinary matter, allowing them to pass through enormous amounts of material virtually undisturbed.

However, when neutrinos occasionally interact with matter in the Antarctic ice, they can produce secondary charged particles that emit detectable flashes of light. IceCube’s instruments record these flashes, allowing scientists to reconstruct information about the incoming neutrinos.

Some dark matter models predict that neutrinos could be produced through dark matter annihilation. Because neutrinos can escape from deep within celestial bodies, detecting them could provide important clues about dark matter accumulating inside planets and stars.

For Jupiter and white dwarf stars elsewhere in the universe, researchers examined another possible signature: excess heat. Although these celestial bodies produce or retain heat through conventional processes, neither Jupiter nor white dwarfs sustains ordinary hydrogen fusion in their interiors. This makes them potentially useful environments for investigating whether dark matter annihilation contributes additional energy.

In their study, the researchers compared observed temperatures with the heating predicted by their dark matter models to determine whether the data could constrain the proposed interactions.

Exploring the Data

By comparing their theoretical calculations with real-world observations, the researchers obtained important null results that could help narrow the search for dark matter. They also found that white dwarfs may be particularly useful for testing dark matter’s electromagnetic properties, while Earth offers promising opportunities to investigate whether dark matter particles carry a small electric charge.

However, the findings come with a significant caveat: they depend on assumptions about dark matter’s properties and distribution that remain uncertain.

One important factor is the amount of dark matter surrounding stars, which has only been estimated for the white dwarfs in the M4 star cluster examined in the study. As more precise measurements become available, the constraints derived from these observations could change.

Looking ahead, the team hopes to expand its investigations to include exoplanets as potential dark matter traps, along with colder white dwarfs, where additional heating from dark matter annihilation might be easier to distinguish from conventional sources.

The paper, “Celestial Probes of Dark Matter Electromagnetic Interactions,” appeared in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics on November 17, 2026.
